title: Managing Someone Who Used to Be Your Peer
script: Bayu: [thoughtful] Sinta, have you got a minute? I need to talk through something awkward, and I'd rather not let it fester any longer.
Sinta: Of course. You've seemed distracted since you got promoted. Is it about managing the team now?
Bayu: [carefully] Partly. It's specifically about managing Danu, who was my closest friend at work right up until three weeks ago.
Sinta: Ah. That's a genuinely difficult transition. What's actually going wrong between you two?
Bayu: [reflective] His deadlines have been slipping, and I keep putting off saying anything, because it feels like betraying a friendship rather than doing my job.
Sinta: Would you have hesitated this long if the underperforming person weren't someone you used to grab lunch with every day?
Bayu: [honestly] Probably not, and that's exactly what's been eating at me. I'm essentially letting our friendship excuse behaviour I'd challenge in anyone else.
Sinta: That's not fair to Danu either, ironically. If everyone else is being held to a standard he's quietly exempt from, he'll never know there's a problem.
Bayu: [gently] When you put it that way, my silence looks less like kindness and more like avoidance dressed up as loyalty.
Sinta: So separate the two conversations. Have the professional one about deadlines clearly and specifically, and let the friendship exist outside of work hours.
Bayu: [calmly] What if he thinks the promotion has changed how I see him, or assumes I'm punishing him somehow for something unrelated?
Sinta: He might feel that initially, but avoiding the conversation would confirm something worse: that you can't be trusted to manage fairly.
Bayu: [encouraging] Fine. I'll ask him for coffee this afternoon, somewhere neutral, and address it directly instead of circling around it indefinitely.
Sinta: Good. Lead with specifics rather than feelings, so it doesn't come across as a personal complaint dressed up as management.
Bayu: [seriously] I suppose I assumed being promoted would feel like gaining authority, not losing the easy comfort of being someone's equal.
Sinta: That discomfort usually fades once people see you're being consistent, not once you stop caring about them personally.
